title: Paella Valenciana
subtitle: The original Valencian rice dish with chicken, rabbit and beans
excerpt: Paella valenciana is the original paella: chicken, rabbit, green beans, butter beans, and rice cooked together in a wide pan with saffron and smoked paprika until the rice absorbs all the stock and forms a crust on the bottom. This crust -- the socarrat -- is the most prized part. The dish has nothing to do with seafood: that is a later variation.
sourceNotes: Paella originates from the rice-growing region of Valencia on the eastern coast of Spain. The name paella refers to the wide, flat, two-handled pan in which it is cooked. The original dish was made by farmers with whatever was to hand: chicken, rabbit, and vegetables from the field. Seafood paella developed later. Paella rice must be a short-grain variety that absorbs stock without becoming sticky -- Bomba or Calasparra rice is ideal. Risotto rice is a reasonable substitute.

content.text: Once the stock goes in, do not stir the paella. Stirring releases starch and produces a gummy rice -- the exact opposite of what you want. The socarrat (bottom crust) forms when the stock has been absorbed and the rice begins to fry in the fat remaining in the pan. You will hear a gentle crackle. After 2 minutes on high heat, the socarrat is done.

Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a wide, shallow pan (at least 36 cm) over high heat. Brown {{chicken-thigh}} chicken pieces well on all sides, about 8 minutes. Push to the edges. Add {{garlic}} garlic and {{tinned-tomatoes}} tomatoes to the centre. Cook for 3 minutes. Stir in {{smoked-paprika}} smoked paprika.

Add {{green-beans}} green beans and {{cannellini-beans}} butter beans. Stir to coat. Add {{arborio-rice}} rice and stir to combine. Pour in {{chicken-stock}} warm stock and the {{saffron}} saffron water. Season with {{salt-table}} salt. Distribute the rice and chicken evenly across the pan. Do not stir again.

Boil hard for 5 minutes, then reduce to a steady simmer for 12 minutes until the stock has been absorbed. Increase the heat to high for 2 minutes to form the socarrat. Listen for a gentle crackling. Remove from the heat, cover with foil or a clean cloth, and rest for 5 minutes. Serve from the pan.

items.symptom: The rice is gummy and sticks together
items.cause: The paella was stirred after the stock was added, releasing starch.
items.fix: Once the stock goes in, do not touch the rice. Spread it flat and leave it. A gummy paella cannot be fixed -- the next batch will be better.

items.symptom: The rice is undercooked and the stock has gone
items.cause: Too much heat, or not enough stock.
items.fix: Add a small amount of warm stock (100 ml at a time) around the edges and cook for a few more minutes. The rice should absorb it.

content.text: Paella comes from Valencia, a flat, irrigated region on the east coast of Spain that has grown rice since the Moorish period. The dish was originally cooked outdoors over a wood fire. The wide pan allows the rice to cook in a thin, even layer, and the wood fire gave it a smoky bottom crust. Valencians are very particular about what is and is not a real paella. Peas, chorizo, seafood mixed with meat, and onion are all considered wrong by Valencian traditionalists -- though these versions are made across the rest of Spain and the world.
